title: China warns it will safeguard its interests after US widens sanctions against Iran
description: China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include
body: China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month. Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US."The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television."We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war.The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade.Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement.With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further.He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response. David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib". "We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate."And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people.Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.

schema.headline: China warns it will safeguard its interests after US widens sanctions against Iran

title: Russian stadium says it won't host Kanye West gigs
description: The Russian stadium that was scheduled to host two shows by Ye, the rapper also known as Kanye West, has said the events will no longer take place.In
body: The Russian stadium that was scheduled to host two shows by Ye, the rapper also known as Kanye West, has said the events will no longer take place.In a social media post, external, St Petersburg's Gazprom Arena said no rental agreement had been signed with the concert promoters. "Accordingly, the concert cannot take place on our site."West would have been the first major Western performer to play Russia since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. The rapper is trying to rehabilitate his image after years of antisemitic remarks, for which he recently apologised.Gazprom Arena acknowledged it had received complaints about West's planned appearance and stressed that it "was not and is not" responsible for his booking.The stadium said in its statement that the sold-out concerts, scheduled for 10 and 11 October, had been organised by the Moscow-based Say Agency. Posting on its Telegram channel, Say Agency said the stadium's announcement had come as a surprise."We learned about [it] at the same time as you did, through the media," the agency wrote. "As of now, the Ye concert has not been canceled," it added in a follow-up message."We are trying to contact the venue to find out the reason for the post and resolve the issue. We will keep you updated."The BBC has contacted West's publicist for a comment on the uncertainty over his Russian shows.In its statement, Say Agency said it announced the concerts earlier this month based "on an official letter that was approved by" Gazprom Arena.The stadium subsequently sent a rental agreement, Say Agency claimed, and the agency acknowledged the contract had not yet been signed but said the deadline to do so did not expire until later this week.Last week, Gazprom Arena had posted enthusiastically about the concerts on social media, calling Ye "the most influential musical artist of our time".Fans reacted to its latest announcement with disappointment."This was the shortest concert of my life," responded one, under Say Agency's Telegram post. "It's a shame that the government is putting obstacles in your way," added another.There is no indication that authorities intervened in the shows, but there has been opposition to West's booking from some Russian politicians.Vitaly Milonov, a notorious conservative lawmaker, suggested the star should perform traditional Russian songs instead of his planned setlist, reflecting the anti-Western views of many nationalists."Maybe after this he'll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person," Milonov added in a video statement.West's antisemitic remarks began in 2022, when he made a series of offensive comments on social media that led to his accounts being suspended. Fashion brands like Adidas and Balenciaga also ended their relationships with the star.The musician went on to declare he was "a Nazi", releasing a song called Heil Hitler and selling T-shirts featuring the swastika.This January, West apologised in a full-page advertisement in the Wall Street Journal, writing: "I am not a Nazi or an antisemite."Reflecting on a "four-month-long manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour", he said he was "deeply mortified" by his actions and that his bipolar disorder meant "you're manic [and] you don't think you're sick".However, some questioned the timing of his statement - which coincided with the release of a new album, Bully, and the start of his world tour.He held his first major concert in the United States in more than five years in Los Angeles in April, but planned shows in England, France, Italy and Poland have been cancelled over his past behaviour. Say Agency acknowledged the controversy in a Telegram post last week, external, but defended its decision to bring West to Russia."Not everything Kanye West said should be forgotten," it said."Many people are talking about Kanye today. Many are trying to criticise him for words spoken during difficult times."But it's easy to judge based on a single statement. It's more difficult to listen to a person who has been changing the industry for decades. We listened, and we want to remind you."

schema.headline: Russian stadium says it won't host Kanye West gigs

title: Government invests £71m to help reopen Devon tungsten mine
description: £71m investment to reopen tungsten mine Image source, Tungsten WestImage caption, The government has invested £71m into Tungsten WestByZhara SimpsonDe
body: £71m investment to reopen tungsten mine Image source, Tungsten WestImage caption, The government has invested £71m into Tungsten WestByZhara SimpsonDevonMore than £70m of public money will be invested into a mining company to help restart production, the Chancellor has said. The Hemerdon tungsten and tin mine in Devon will receive up to £71m from the National Wealth Fund to resume operations at the mine near Plymouth.Chancellor John Healey said it meant Britain could tap into one of the world's largest deposit of the mineral which is used in steel, electronics and aerospace industries. The government said it would ringfence 50% of the production for use in Britain.The financing consists of a £36m equity investment alongside up to £35m of lending to help Tungsten West restart production.Image source, Tungsten WestImage caption, The National Wealth Fund also invested in Cornish Metals in January 2025The National Wealth Fund said the funding supported its continued growth and renewal of mining in south-west England, building on its most recent investment in Cornish Metals to help it reopen South Crofty tin mine in January 2025. Healey said: "We are living in a more dangerous world, which is why backing British industry is more important than ever before. That is what this deal does."National Wealth Fund chief executive Oliver Holbourn said Hemerdon had the "largest deposits of tungsten in the world right on our doorstep".He said the increasing demand for tungsten was being driven by its use in defence, aerospace, next generation energy and electronics. Chief executive of Tungsten West Jeff Court said the mine was a "world class, low cost and long life tungsten and tin resource".Image source, Tungsten WestImage caption, Jeff Court said the mines were a long-term creator of economic benefits for the South West Court said: "It is extremely important to us that we prioritise UK requirements for this critical metal to support domestic demand. "Hemerdon will be a long-term creator of economic benefits for the South West, including the generation of a significant number of direct and indirect jobs."He said the government support was ensuring critical minerals produced at the mine would underpin the UK's national interests for the "long term".The company said the existing infrastructure and previously-operating mine resulted in competitive costs and a shorter route to production. It said the target was to "ramp up to full scale production" in 2027.The government's business secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the investment was a "major vote of confidence" in its critical minerals sector and a step forward in the Prime Minister's plans to "reindustrialise Britain", while supporting skilled jobs across Devon.Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

schema.headline: Government invests £71m to help reopen Devon tungsten mine

title: HPV home-testing kits now available for women who have missed cervical screening
description: Gem Sofianos-Boorman, 39, said her experience shows how important the screening is. She was diagnosed with cervical cancer at 28, following screening,
body: Gem Sofianos-Boorman, 39, said her experience shows how important the screening is. She was diagnosed with cervical cancer at 28, following screening, and says it was the last thing she expected, given she was young, healthy and had no symptoms.She had surgery to remove the cancerous cells plus lymph nodes from her abdomen and pelvis to stop it spreading."Looking back, I truly believe that going to my screening appointment saved my life. My cancer was found early, which allowed me to have treatment before it spread."That's why it's great news that the NHS is making it more accessible for some people to take part in screening."Cervical cancer often doesn't cause any symptoms until the disease is more advanced and harder to treat."If you receive an invite to cervical screening, or an offer of a self-testing kit, please don't ignore it - it could save your life."Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women's health, said: "Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game-changer – making it easier than ever for them to get tested."There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test."Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "Cervical cancer is preventable - but that's why we want to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening."The kits contain a swab, similar to a long cotton, bud which is used to collect a sample from the vagina.It is then sent back to the NHS and if high-risk HPV is found, individuals will be invited to book a follow-up cervical screening appointment.High-risk HPV increases the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not mean a woman will automatically develop it.Trials of the self-testing in London suggest it could lead to one in 10 women to come forward for screening – boosting uptake by around 400,000 a year.Other parts of the UK are also looking at introducing self-testing.Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years – or more frequently if HPV is detected.Through a combination of HPV vaccination, which is offered to teenagers, and improved screening, the NHS is hoping to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.The NHS says cervical screening appointments with a clinician is still the best way to prevent cancer – and even if you have missed an appointment you can still come forward for one.

schema.headline: HPV home-testing kits now available for women who have missed cervical screening

title: Why some US restaurants are banning tips
description: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tipsImage source, Caroline KraetzerImage caption, Caroline Kraetzer no longer get
body: 'What you see is what you pay' - why some US restaurants are banning tipsImage source, Caroline KraetzerImage caption, Caroline Kraetzer no longer gets tips but her salary is double the normBySuzanne Bearne Wine waiter Caroline Kraetzer earns $40 (£30) an hour, double what most service staff in San Francisco are paid but then it costs a lot to eat at her restaurant.At a set price of $140 (£100) per person, La Cigale is one of a small number of US restaurants charging higher prices so it can pay high salaries - and it doesn't allow tips.It tells customers: "What you see is what you pay. We do not accept tips, your kind words and return visits will suffice."Kraetzer says it is good to no longer be "reliant on the generosity of strangers to pay the bills".While waiting staff at other restaurants can make a lot of money from tips, she says "you're often there two hours before service, and again when you're closing after the guests have left, so you are making minimum wage during that time".Fairer for staff?On the other side of the US, Rachel Miller, chef and owner of Nightshade Noodle Bar in the town Lynn, Massachusetts, moved to a tip-free model five years ago when they reopened after the Covid-19 pandemic.Her motivation was to make it fairer for the kitchen staff. "The people breaking their backs and minds in the kitchen - often the least visible and the least celebrated - were taking home a fraction of what the front staff made on tips for the same hours," she says.Miller says she found it "deeply unsettling" to see higher tips going to white male staff and lower tips to everyone else. "Tipping lets guests, consciously or not, pay people differently based on gender, race, or sexuality and I was not willing to let that decide my team's income."To pay the staff higher wages, Miller also increased prices at the French-Vietnamese restaurant. Its tasting menus now start from $102 (£75) for seven courses before 18:00, and $126 (£92) for nine courses."Our prices are higher than a comparable restaurant's because they carry the full cost of paying people properly," says Miller. "That is the trade, and I stand behind it."Image source, Alyssa BlumsteinImage caption, Rachel Miller says that banning tips is fairer for her kitchen staffTip-free can mean higher pricesYet not every restaurant that has switched to a tipless model has made a success of it, as sometimes customers don't appreciate the higher menu prices.Talulla in Cambridge, Massachusetts, dropped tips in 2020 so it could pay staff more equitably, only to then switch back in September of last year."We tried to keep our non-tipping model simply by raising our menu prices 23%, but we were only able to sustain this through the winter months," says co-owner Danielle Ayer."Operating a non-tipped restaurant is more expensive overall," adds Ayer. This is because tips don't count as part of a restaurant's revenues, but higher menu prices do. So if a venue increases prices to pay staff more, its revenues go up accordingly, and it must pay more sales tax.William Michael Lynn, professor of food and beverage management at Cornell University and author of The Psychology of Tipping, says the problem of going tip-free is that customers struggle to get their heads around the maths."Higher menu prices make dining out seem more expensive because people do not adequately take into account that they are no longer tipping," he says. "It leads to lower demand."Image source, Amanda CohenImage caption, Amanda Cohen says customers are pleased when they realise they don't have to tipIn New York, vegetarian restaurant Dirt Candy was one of the very first to ban tipping back in 2015. "I wanted to make it more equal for everybody," says chef and owner Amanda Cohen, who now pays her staff about $30 an hour.She says that many customers "are pleasantly surprised when they realise they don't have to tip 20% on top".Cassidy Van der Kamp is a filmmaker whose YouTube documentary Tipless was inspired by her own experience of working in a restaurant in Oakland, California which went tip-free.While some other servers left, Van der Kamp, who was originally paid about $10 an hour plus tips, decided to stay and earned $21 per hour after the change."I had stability for the first time as I knew what I was earning… and I didn't need to look at a low tip and think what did I do wrong?"'Tipping fatigue'While Van der Kamp liked the move, Lynn says that a huge challenge of moving to a gratuity-free system is that it can be difficult to attract and retain waiting staff who like getting tips.However, given the growth of what has been called "tipping fatigue" – people being increasingly annoyed at having to pay high tips – will more restaurants stop the practice?"Despite tip-fatigue, I do not think tipping is going to be eliminated on widescale anytime soon because the economic disadvantages of eliminating tipping outweigh the advantages," says Lynn.Back at Nightshade Noodle Bar, Miller doesn't regret her decision. "The clearest measure is that staff stay."Turnover in this industry is brutal, and we have people who have been here since we made the change. It has proven to be highly valued by my guests and team."

schema.headline: Why some US restaurants are banning tips

title: Andy Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises in autumn Budget
description: Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the upcoming autumn Budget, saying he "won't be unrealistic" about the "challenging" state of public
body: Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the upcoming autumn Budget, saying he "won't be unrealistic" about the "challenging" state of public finances.The prime minister said he would take a "careful approach" to the economy, and defended his previously announced cost of living pledges as funded spending commitments.Burnham became prime minister in July promising to give people breathing space and help with the cost of living, but questions remain over how major policies such as social care reforms will be funded.Experts have previously warned that he and Chancellor John Healey will have little financial room to manoeuvre in their first Budget on 28 October.Speaking during his first visit to Ukraine, Burnham said the policies announced so far including capping bus fares at £2 and cutting VAT on household electricity bills were "the first steps that I've felt able to make", and were doable because he was able to reprioritise funding from elsewhere."I took the decision early on that digital ID wasn't the top priority for now. And so we've reprioritised funding to other priorities," he said in an interview with ITV.Asked if the public needed to accept some of the new policies would have to be paid for in tax rises, Burnham said they wouldn't necessarily have to accept that.Pushed on whether he would need to raise taxes to cover spending gaps, he said: "I will always take a careful approach to things. I ran Greater Manchester for 10 years and we ran a very tight ship with rock solid finances."Nothing will change as I come into this role as prime minister. I won't take risks with people's jobs or their livelihoods or their family finances."I will try to help them in whatever way I can, I have already done some things that will help them."Burnham previously told the BBC he accepts his earlier announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.Speaking during his first official overseas visit on Monday, he said while he would do what he could, "I won't be unrealistic and people really need to understand that."We are in a challenging position, whatever I do will be carefully thought through, it will be funded and there will be more to come as we go into the autumn."Last week official figures showed the the government borrowed more than expected in July, despite a record month for income tax receipts.Inflation also reached a four-month high of 2.9% in July and is expected to rise further due to the ongoing impact of the Iran war, which has hit energy prices and fuel costs.Experts have warned Burnham and Healey that they need to either raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere as pressure on the public finances has left no room for extra borrowing.Both the prime minister and chancellor have vowed to stick to the fiscal rules set by former chancellor Rachel Reeves. The rules are designed to ensure day-to-day spending is funded through tax revenue by the end of the Parliament, and to reduce debt as a proportion of GDP.Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry, said business owners wanted to create opportunities for young people but "the cost of employing people has gone up so much"."The business leaders I speak to say that the cost of doing business has gone up so much that it's holding them back from creating opportunities," she told the Today programme.She said targeted support for businesses would create "more growth and more opportunities that saves money for the government and ultimately leads to higher tax receipts".

schema.headline: Andy Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises in autumn Budget

title: How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump
description: What leverage does Canada, which sells about 70% of its goods to the US, actually have in this spiralling trade dispute with its southern neighbour, w
body: What leverage does Canada, which sells about 70% of its goods to the US, actually have in this spiralling trade dispute with its southern neighbour, who also happens to be the world's largest economy?Canada is the top customer for 26 US states, including Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin. And it is in the top three for 45 of the 50 American states, suggesting Prime Minister Mark Carney has room to manoeuvre in a trade fight.For now, Carney's planned Canadian retaliatory duties are strategic "dollar-for-dollar" countermeasures focused on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, electronics, pulp and paper - though the list is still being finalised.Polls suggest a majority of Canadians would be unhappy if his government went in the other direction and made significant concessions to the US. That sentiment is shared by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of Trump's most vocal critics north of the border, who responded to the tariff threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass".Canada's Finance Department said additional measures to protect workers and businesses would be announced on Tuesday.Here are some areas where Canada can apply economic pressure.Carney noted on Saturday that Canada supplies the vast majority of US natural gas and electricity imports and about 60% of crude oil imports."I don't think they want us to stop sending any of that energy," he said.Squeezing the US on energy is not in the current countermeasures, although various political officials have said explicitly it wasn't ruled out - and not all provincial premiers have been keen to use that leverage.Ford, whose Ontario province is home to Canada's auto manufacturing industry,  is open to how far the dispute could go and said that an "energy surcharge is on the table".He briefly floated a 25% surcharge in 2025 on all electricity exports to the United States, which his government estimated would have impacted 1.5 million homes and businesses in Michigan, Minnesota and New York.The country is also a major source of important commodities including potash - a product in fertiliser for which Canada is the world's top supplier."I'd love to see [Trump] run cars without any oil. I'll love to see him grow vegetables and fruit without the potash," Ford said on Monday. "President Trump underestimates us, and that's the biggest mistake."Canada also has significant reserves of critical minerals like lithium, nickel and graphite.The US is Canada's top destination for overall mineral exports, another point where Ottawa could apply pressure.Ford here also took the lead, saying in an interview with the Associated Press that the US  "won't get a grain of sand out of Ontario".Canada has already proven that it can cause economic pain in the US.Even before trade talks broke down, a decision by most provinces to ban US alcohol from liquor store shelves - in response to the first wave of US tariffs early last year - dealt a devastating blow to that industry in the US.American wine had a significant collapse in exports, one the Wine Institute called the "most significant market disruption in decades".US wine exports to Canada fell 78% year over year, a $357m (C$494m; £261m) loss in export value, according to government data. The distillers association reported similar numbers - saying provincial bans have caused exports of American spirits to drop by more than 70%.That boycott remains in place in 11 of the 13 Canadian provinces and territories. The ban is a point of significant frustration for the Trump administration.While that alcohol boycott has been put in place by political leaders, there are also grassroots decisions by many Canadians that have hurt their neighbour's economy - such as avoiding travel to the US.Even with a slight uptick in road trips to the US in April, Canadians made 800,000 fewer trips that month compared to the same time in 2024, before Trump returned to office, according to national data.The travel boycott has meant a loss of about C$3.3bn ($2.35bn; £1.75bn) in revenue for the US last year. Some American cities and states have appealed for Canadians to return through targeted advertisements and special deals.Timing and Canadian political will could also be a tool for negotiations.Canadians know they will feel economic pain in this dispute - financial analysts estimated the most recent tariffs of 50% on about $20bn of Canadian imports could trim between 0.3% to 0.6% off the country's GDP in the short term.Still, a majority in the country broadly back Ottawa's decision to drive a hard bargain against the Trump administration, and other Canadian political leaders have shown a united front.A weekend poll from Angus Reid indicated that some 76% of Canadians support Ottawa's decision to walk away from trade negotiations even as they worry for their own job security.The US midterm elections are fast approaching, with the economy front and centre for voters and the Republican hold on Congress looking tenuous.Two of the biggest Senate races are in Michigan and Maine, which both border Canada and send most of their exports there.The Yale Budget Lab calculates that under current law, Trump's global tariffs will cost American households about $1,100 annually.Any further increase in the costs of goods and the wider impact of the trade dispute on businesses could further sour the American public on the economy.On Monday, Carney said that US workers will be hurt by Trump's most recent threat to increase tariff on autos and auto parts from Canada to 50% after 1 January."What is the message sent out to the workers in Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Alabama? These workers depend absolutely on Canada, their largest consumer," he said, adding that Canada buys more American cars than the EU and other countries.On CNN on Monday, British Columbia Premier David Eby noted US consumers will see the impact of the US tariffs in any number of goods."If you're building a new home, on plywood, if you're replacing your floor, on veneers, if you're getting married, on cut flowers, if you're going out fishing, on fishing poles," he said."It is a bizarre policy for Americans. It's going to hurt them."Ford, one of the most vocal Canadian leaders opposing the Trump administration's tariffs, also did not rule out specifically targeting Republican US states with retaliatory measures and "making sure America's economy feels the pain".As for the coming midterms, Ford said: "If I were allowed to, I'd be down there door-knocking".

schema.headline: How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump

title: Savinho: Tottenham sign winger from Manchester City for £75m
description: Tottenham have signed Brazil winger Savinho from Manchester City for an initial £75m. The 22-year-old has joined Spurs on a long-term contract with Ro
body: Tottenham have signed Brazil winger Savinho from Manchester City for an initial £75m. The 22-year-old has joined Spurs on a long-term contract with Roberto de Zerbi's side potentially paying a further £10m in add-ons.Savinho's move to north London has been more than 12 months in the making, with Spurs failing in a bid to sign him last summer.Savinho opted to remain at Etihad Stadium, but his game time was limited under Pep Guardiola last term when he made just seven Premier League starts."It's taken a while but I'm very happy to be here," said Savinho."It's a wonderful opportunity at a brilliant club with one of the best managers in the world."As soon as I spoke to the head coach I knew I had to come. He told me he wants to help me reach the highest level, and I believe we can do that together, as a team."Savinho joined City from French side Troyes in a £30.8m deal in 2024 and has made 84 appearances for the club in total, scoring seven goals and providing 16 assists.The Brazil international joins Spurs following the arrivals of Mateus Fernandes from West Ham, Sandro Tonali from Newcastle and Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton this summer for a combined £312m.Spurs have also brought in defenders Marcos Senesi and Andrew Robertson in on free transfers and goalkeeper Martin Dubravka.Tottenham's new addition will be known as Savio - his first name - rather than Savinho, as he was during his two years at City.During the winger's previous spell at Girona he had Savio on his shirt, but he opted for a change when he moved to the Premier League.He said he hoped that decision would "bring him luck" - having had Savinho on the back of his jersey for his Brazil debut - but has now reverted to Savio."Savio is a player who brings energy, imagination and quality in wide positions. He has the courage to attack defenders and the ability to change a game with his creativity," said De Zerbi.City also remain in advanced talks to sell Egypt forward Omar Marmoush to Spurs, and sources with knowledge of the situation say there is a "good chance" the deal gets completed before the 1 September transfer deadline.Savinho's involvement for City fell sharply last season after the club signed winger Antoine Semenyo from Bournemouth in January.He played 821 Premier League minutes, scoring once and providing one assist, while featuring in only 31% of City's available minutes across all competitions.That was a significant drop from the previous campaign, when he played 54% of City's minutes.Yet his 2024-25 numbers show why Tottenham are prepared to invest heavily in him. Savinho registered eight Premier League assists that season, all from open play, despite playing only 1,773 minutes. Only five players recorded more from open play.On a per-90 basis, he ranked third for open-play assists with 0.41, while only Mohamed Salah created more chances per 90 than Savinho's 2.2.His biggest threat, though, came from carrying the ball. Among Premier League players with at least 1,000 minutes in 2024-25, only Jeremy Doku averaged more progressive carries of at least 10 metres than Savinho's 6.8 per 90.Savinho also led the division for carries followed by a chance created, averaging 1.3 per 90, while only Son Heung-min ended a carry with an assist more frequently. He completed 2.6 dribbles per 90 with a 51% success rate and used those carries to draw defenders towards him before releasing team-mates.That ability was even more evident during his breakout season at Girona. Savinho played 2,989 minutes in La Liga in 2023-24, with 65% of them coming on the left wing. He scored nine goals, supplied eight assists and established himself as one of the division's most dangerous one-against-one players.At City his role shifted. Across his two Premier League seasons, his most common position was on the right, accounting for 36% of his minutes, compared with 20% on the left. That versatility could matter at Spurs.

schema.headline: Savinho: Tottenham sign winger from Manchester City for £75m

title: Billy Boston: Legendary Wigan, Wales and GB winger dies aged 92
description: Boston would go on to score 24 tries in 31 appearances for Great Britain and was part of the side that won the 1960 World Cup, scoring a try in the fi
body: Boston would go on to score 24 tries in 31 appearances for Great Britain and was part of the side that won the 1960 World Cup, scoring a try in the final as they beat Australia 10-3 at Odsal Stadium in Bradford.Boston finished his playing career as a second row with Blackpool Borough.In all, Boston scored 571 tries in his career - a total surpassed only by Australian legend Brian Bevan in top-class rugby league -  and is one of the truly great British rugby league players.After his retirement from the game, Boston ran the Griffin Hotel close to Wigan's Central Park Ground where one of the stands was named after the Welshman.Boston was among the first players inducted into the Rugby League Hall of Fame in 1988 and is one of five rugby league players to be included in a statue at Wembley Stadium. He is immortalised in two more statues, in Wigan where he is an adopted son and in his home city of Cardiff.Boston was appointed an MBE in 1986, and was among the first to be inducted into the Welsh Sports Hall of Fame, external when it was launched in 1990.In 2025, and having being diagnosed with dementia, he was awarded the highest honour, a knighthood by King Charles.His death comes just weeks after the passing of his wife, Lady Joan.Tributes have been led by Wigan owner Mike Danson, who said: "Billy Boston was everybody's hero, including my Mum's."His achievements in rugby league were extraordinary, and his knighthood was a fitting recognition of a career that brought great credit to Wigan and to the game."But Billy's legacy was not simply what he achieved. It was the humility with which he carried it. Despite everything he accomplished, he remained a quiet, dignified and deeply respected man."He leaves behind an example that will endure for generations. Our thoughts are with his family and those closest to him."A great man, and a true Wigan legend. He will be remembered with pride and affection."In a released statement, Wales Rugby League said: "Today, rugby league has lost one of its greatest-ever players, Wales has lost one of its finest sporting sons, and our sport has lost a truly special gentleman."The WRU also paid tribute, calling Boston "One of the best loved and most iconic figures in the history of Welsh sport."Matt Newsum, BBC rugby league commentatorIt is testament to the star power of Sir Billy Boston that even 56 years after he last graced a rugby pitch, young fans are fully aware of the legend that is the Welshman from Cardiff's Tiger Bay.He had a uniquely unifying effect on a normally partisan and tribal rugby league community. Revered naturally in Wigan, his adopted home, but you won't hear a boo or jeer at mention of Boston anywhere - not even at sworn rivals St Helens where they appreciate a good footballer when they see one.The sepia footage and slow shutter-speeds of the cameras that captured the magic of his playing days simply cannot dull his brilliance; whether it's bustling over for another try in cherry and white hoops at Wembley or crushing the Aussies at the Sydney Cricket Ground, Boston is a blur of speed, footwork and power.Wing or centre, a wonderful finisher and a player whose innate talents were honed on those tough streets of his district - one that also produced fellow pioneers Roy Francis and Colin Dixon.Many a fan will have drunk at the pub which provided some of his post-playing focus, the Griffin Hotel, close to the Central Park ground he scored so many of his 571 tries on - the best strike rate of any British player.Still a regular visitor to Wigan games right up to his death, it was always a beautiful moment when the cameras found him, the crowd spotting him on the screen bursting into cheer, and the realisation creeping over his face in the shape of a smile.It will take some getting used to, the empty seat at the Brick. He will be missed but certainly not forgotten.

schema.headline: Billy Boston: Legendary Wigan, Wales and GB winger dies aged 92

title: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workersByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing, Hangzhou and Chengdu"I
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workersByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing, Hangzhou and Chengdu"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.Image caption, Students learning robotics at the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of many new vocational schoolsIt is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.Image caption, More than two millions robots work alongside people in China's factories On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code."Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."Image caption, Pang Kai is part of the research and development teamA shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages."In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotor.Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."Image caption, Machines are part of every step in making Leapmotor's EVsChina has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand."China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics."If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.Image caption, Chinese innovation is powering the country's factories faster than expected   And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says."It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption. It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

schema.headline: China's humanoid robots are stealing the show, but a quieter machine revolution is unfolding

title: Food influencers v critics: Why credibility counts
description: Image source, Oscar BostockImage caption, "Creators certainly have an influence on how people go out to eat, for sure," says Bristol influencer Oscar
body: Image source, Oscar BostockImage caption, "Creators certainly have an influence on how people go out to eat, for sure," says Bristol influencer Oscar BostockByJasmine Ketibuah-FoleyWest of EnglandWhen stuck for ideas about where to eat on a Friday night or torn between takeaways, more and more people are turning to social media and their favourite content creators for inspiration.Research by one Bristol food writer has raised questions about transparency, with some creators guaranteeing positive coverage in advance and offering not to make clear their review was in exchange for a free meal.Those promises of good reviews were made before they had eaten a bite - or realised the restaurant they had been asked to promote did not exist.So can diners trust influencers to give an honest opinion and what is their role in shaping where we eat? We asked people in the food scene to share their thoughts.Meg Houghton-Gilmour, food writer and founder of The Bristol Sauce, undertook a two-part research piece, external into the world of food influencing when she created a website and social media account for a fake Japanese restaurant "coming soon to Bristol". She messaged 48 influencers asking how much they would charge to make content, what would guarantee positive coverage and whether they would declare it an advert.After receiving 33 responses, she said the prices quoted by influencers varied widely. Some said they would post in exchange for free food and drink, without an extra payment on top - and five of those said they would post without labelling the content as an advert.UK advertising rules state paid posts must be clearly marked with #ad or a platform's paid partnership feature. This includes free meals in exchange for posts.Houghton-Gilmour added the requests she sent out had created a swell of "misleading" positive noise on social media around the upcoming opening."I realised how insular and repetitive it is. Everyone going to the same places, saying the same thing," she said.Image source, Meg Houghton-GilmourImage caption, Meg Houghton-Gilmour said her research offered "a fascinating insight" into the world of influencersWith more than 135,000 followers on Instagram, external and millions of views on TikTok, external, Oscar Bostock, also known as Bos Finesse, is a driving force as a food creator in Bristol and said becoming an influencer was a "no-brainer"."There are food creators in the social media space, like myself, who do have a lot of credibility. But we need to respect the culture a bit as well."You'll never beat the people that write about food for a living. I don't really like to review and criticise food - I'll leave that to the professionals. "At the same time, you need people here like myself to just celebrate food," he adds.Bostock says authenticity is very important to him, and told the BBC there are many places he has said no to reviewing or reflecting. "It's worth explaining it, being paid for a restaurant to say, 'this is good' is completely different to being  paid to promote a new menu or venue. "I feel very strongly about it, anywhere I work with had to be a place I actually valued and would visit in my own time."Image source, Jay RaynerImage caption, Consumers needed to know whether someone had paid for the meal they were talking about, said food critic Jay RaynerFood critic Jay Rayner, who writes for the Financial Times, believes his role is to write "as interesting, entertaining [and] truthful column" as he can."I don't think there's much truth in the idea that the newspaper critic is dead," he said. "What I see happening is an awful lot more media around restaurants, full stop."I know, anecdotally, that a good review from me still results in many bookings, which is lovely - but it's not actually a concern of mine."He said people sometimes ask if influencers "pose a challenge to what you do"."My response is, 'only if it's better than what I do'," said Rayner, stressing his authority as a critic is not unassailable. "I do not have a right to my lofty perch."Rayner said newspapers such as the Financial Times would "pick up the bill" for critics writing reviews, whereas a lot of influencers were invited to eat for nothing, which is something consumers should be aware of."That does undermine the credibility of the review," he said. "[But] you know, we're all celebrating the culture of eating food and eating out."Image source, Adam ArmstrongImage caption, Chef Adam Armstrong said influencers, like critics, offer an opinion which "you don't have to look at"Adam Armstrong, head chef at Bath's Emberwood, said the sort of promotion restaurants received from influencers was something the industry would have been "screaming out for" years ago."If you make a bit of noise here or there, it just puts you on the map," he said.He acknowledged many people had a "negative" view of food creators, but added: "People give them too much reverence in the first place. They're just people with an opinion."The Nook Cheltenham, in Gloucestershire, has worked hard at being Instagram-friendly, currently boasting more than 11,000 followers.Director and founder Edward Surman said: "Social media is a place where brands can alter their own story - where it's not moved around by the press."Surman maintains influencers are not replacing food critics, but more of an "augmentation". Image source, Baljinder Kaur Sangha-GillImage caption, Baljinder Kaur Gill said influencers had opened up the conversation about foodWiltshire-based food influencer Baljinder Kaur Sangha-Gill, also known as The Authentic Punjabee, says her pages have moved beyond a list of recommendations and have come to represent a community of friends."Influencers haven't replaced critics. We've just opened the conversation about food," she said."Years ago, when you were looking for a restaurant or recipe, you'd wait for the Sunday paper. Now you can just go onto TikTok."But she cautions not everything on social media is reliable."People will get free things to promote something. You've got to be aware of that. I'm very careful with that, I don't lie to my followers," she added.Following her research, Houghton-Gilmour added: "Influencers are a symptom of the society and tech world we live in - not the problem. It's the tech billionaires making it unclear what's an ad and what's not."She said the problem was not people making content but the lack of transparency, although she accepted that was not true of all influencers.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Bristol

schema.headline: Food influencers v critics: Why credibility counts

title: Asbestos cancer killed mum in her 40s – was her school to blame?
description: Figure caption, 'Mum died young from asbestos - now we, as a family, want justice'ByWill FyfeWales Impact and Angharad ThomasBBC WalesUpdated 1 hour a
body: Figure caption, 'Mum died young from asbestos - now we, as a family, want justice'ByWill FyfeWales Impact and Angharad ThomasBBC WalesUpdated 1 hour agoWhen Caroline Bryan was enjoying high school with friends in the early '90s, she would never have imagined replaying those memories in her final weeks, while searching for answers about her terminal condition.The mum was 46 when she died from mesothelioma, an incurable cancer linked to asbestos exposure.As she came to terms with her difficult diagnosis, Caroline's belief was the only place she could have encountered asbestos was during her time at school decades earlier.Her family blame the local authority that ran Caroline's school for her death and are taking legal action. Cardiff council said it would be inappropriate to comment on legal proceedings in progress."She never had the sort of career that would have exposed her to asbestos," said Caroline's daughter Brooklyn."We never lived in any houses that would have had asbestos in."Caroline was mostly a stay at home mum and the family had not heard of mesothelioma before, but quickly learned it likely came from asbestos fibres she will have unknowingly breathed in many years before.Image source, Brooklyn BryanImage caption, Brooklyn Bryan says she remembers her mum as a "kind and caring person" who would go "above and beyond for anybody""Before she passed, she contacted a solicitor," added Brooklyn."She wanted justice - not just for herself, but to stop anyone else going through the same thing."The 26-year-old said her world "turned upside down" when she found out her mum had incurable cancer. Brooklyn said after looking back through her mum's life, they had begun to believe she had been exposed to asbestos at her old high school, the old Fitzalan site in Cardiff.The family's legal team helped to uncover council documents that they say show asbestos was used "quite extensively" at the site during Caroline's time there in the 1990s."Mum mentioned that the building wasn't in good condition," said Brooklyn.Image source, Brooklyn BryanImage caption, Caroline Bryan was 45 years old when she noticed she was having breathing difficulties "Things like ceiling tiles were broken. There was dust and debris when things were disturbed, though at the time she didn't know what it was."Caroline had only gone to the doctors because she had noticed a shortness of breath. In her mid 40s, she was far younger than most mesothelioma patients. Doctors had initially told Caroline she could have a few years left – but she passed away just three months after her diagnosis, aged 46."I was 23," said Brooklyn."Suddenly, I had to take over everything—running the house, paying bills, cooking, cleaning. She had always looked after me, so I wasn't used to doing those things. I was essentially forced into adulthood overnight. It was very difficult."Losing your mum, who is your main support system, at that age is incredibly hard. Now she's gone, I feel I have to continue this [fight] for her."Caroline's family are bringing a High Court claim against Cardiff council over her death, with the case set to be heard in early 2027.Image caption, Brooklyn Bryan believes her mum was exposed to asbestos as a teenager at secondary school"The council's own documents show that asbestos was used quite extensively in that school," said Phillip Gower from Redkite Solicitors, who are representing the family."The buildings were in pretty poor condition, with damage to the walls around the doors, the floor tiles, the ceiling tiles."Cardiff Council said it would "not be appropriate" to comment on Caroline's case, but it had recognised the "devastating impact" of mesothelioma on patients and families. "We would like to reassure parents, staff and the wider public that the management of asbestos in Cardiff council buildings, including schools, is taken extremely seriously," added a spokesperson. Many primary and secondary schools were built using asbestos, a common building material until its dangers became clear, and it was banned in the UK in 1999.Most schools still contain some asbestos and authorities must regularly inspect it to check it has not been damaged and at risk of releasing tiny fibres into the air, which can cause cancers like mesothelioma.A Freedom of Information request by BBC Wales suggested more than three-quarters of schools in Wales still contained asbestos.Responses from 20 of Wales' 22 local authorities showed 76% of primary schools and 81% of secondary schools had asbestos containing materials (ACMs).Image caption, Fitzalan High School pupils were taught at the same site Caroline attended from 1964 until the 1,800-pupil school moved location in 2023Mesothelioma is the 20th most common type of cancer in the UK, responsible for 2,200 deaths a year, according to Cancer Research UK.It can develop from a single asbestos fibre lodged in the lungs, often unknowingly breathed in many decades earlier.It is more common in men, particularly those who have worked in heavy industry or trades where they would have regular contact with asbestos. Most deaths with the disease happen when people are in their 80s.However, an epidemiologist who has spent decades studying mesothelioma rates, said there were two "concerning epidemiological observations" coming from more recent data."First, the number of mesothelioma cases per year [in people] under the age of 40 in Britain has increased over the last five or six years - it has increased from 2.5 cases per year to five cases per year," said Prof Julian Peto. "The second thing is that there is a slightly but significantly increased mesothelioma risk in female teachers."Peto said the findings were "not conclusive" but did "raise concern".Image source, Brooklyn BryanImage caption, Brooklyn Bryan says her mum Caroline could make "any situation better"He said there were two likely causes. Either the removal of large amounts of asbestos in schools in the 1980s had accidentally exposed more people to its dangerous fibres – or asbestos in the buildings was deteriorating and releasing more fibres over time, exposing them to later generations of pupils and teachers.Peto said more data was needed to see what was happening – but depending on the answer it could mean more asbestos needs to be removed from schools or that removing it could be the very thing causing the exposure.Often, when someone is diagnosed with mesothelioma they are given a list of solicitors to contact by medical staff so they can look into whether they are due compensation."We are now seeing more women, most of whom cannot readily identify where they could have been exposed to asbestos," said Richard Green from Hugh James Solicitors."What we are also starting to see is a number of younger people who are suffering with mesothelioma. In the last 12 months or so, we've definitely seen an increase in the number of people coming forward who are under 50."Green, a partner in the firm's asbestos litigation team, said they had seen three mesothelioma clients under 40 years old in the past few months – but that it was still exceptionally rare to see anyone under 50 with the disease.He said until around a decade ago most cases were men who had spent their careers working with asbestos – but his firm now considers claims from people who believe they were exposed in schools, either as teachers or pupils.Helen Wilson said it was "devastating" to hear her sister Linda Langhelt had been diagnosed with mesothelioma.Image source, Helen WilsonImage caption, Linda Langhelt's family believe she could have been exposed to asbestos while working as a teacher, decades before her death from cancerThe retired science teacher, who spent her career working in Cardiff and Essex, had gone to see her GP about a shortness of breath thinking it could be "heart problems" before being given her diagnosis."The hospital said she could have contracted it 20 or 30 years before," said her younger sister Helen."The horrible thing about mesothelioma is that you haven't a clue that you've got it until it's too late."Helen said that as a biology teacher, Linda knew exactly what her diagnosis meant – but stayed "stoic" until the end.She died aged 82, 18 months after finding out about her mesothelioma."Every one of us has been in buildings from time to time that have asbestos in them," said Helen.The Welsh government said the safety of pupils and staff was of "paramount importance"."We continue to support local authorities through investment in school buildings, practical guidance and close collaboration with the Health and Safety Executive and Ystadau Cymru to ensure schools remain safe, modern and fit for purpose," said a spokesperson. Cardiff Council said that it had "robust and well-established" plans to manage asbestos in its buildings. "Council buildings are surveyed, asbestos records are maintained and regularly reviewed, and checks are carried out to monitor the condition of any known asbestos-containing materials," said a spokesperson."We remain committed to providing safe environments for pupils, staff and visitors and will continue to manage asbestos in accordance with all current legal requirements and recognised best practice."Get in touchHave you been affected by issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: Asbestos cancer killed mum in her 40s – was her school to blame?

title: Ask CricViz: Who has best DRS record and are left-handers better?
description: During England's first Test against Pakistan, we asked BBC Sport readers to send statistical questions for our colleagues at CricViz.Our new feature,
body: During England's first Test against Pakistan, we asked BBC Sport readers to send statistical questions for our colleagues at CricViz.Our new feature, Ask CricViz, is here to help and we can reveal the first selection of answers below.Please note that all stats in Tests are inclusive of the recent Australia v Bangladesh Test in Mackay, but do not include stats from the ongoing Sri Lanka v India Test in Colombo.Graham, Hastings: Against Pakistan, Josh Tongue took two wickets in two balls but missed out on his hat-trick. What is the 'conversion rate' from having two in two, to going on and getting the hat-trick?CricViz: In Tests where such data is available in our database, there have been 1,355 occasions where a bowler has taken wickets in two consecutive balls, with only 43 (3.2%) of them converted to a hat-trick.There have been a total of 49 hat-tricks in Test history but we have the ball-by-ball details for 43 of them.Across his Test career, Josh Tongue has had two wickets in two balls on four occasions and yet no hat-tricks. The four instances include the two occasions in the last Test versus Pakistan at Headingley, once in the Ashes Test at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in December 2025, and against India at Headingley in June 2025.Here's another interesting bit: Australia's Mitchell Starc has taken wickets in two consecutive balls on 17 occasions in Tests but is yet to register a hat-trick.Charles Dennett, Lichfield: When Joe Root was involved in a 50-run partnership with Jordan Cox, it made me think that he must be close to being the player involved in the most 50-run partnerships with the greatest number of distinct batting partners. Is this true?CricViz: You're spot on with your observation. In the partnership of 150 with Jordan Cox at Headingley, Joe Root has now registered 50-plus run partnerships with 45 distinct partners in Test, the joint-most - tied with Shivnarine Chanderpaul from West Indies.Also interestingly, that partnership with Jordan Cox was the 88th time Joe Root has been involved in a 100-plus partnership, the joint-most in Test history on par with Rahul Dravid from India.Harvey, Dartford: After hearing about Ollie Robinson's terrific stats with balls bowled hitting the stumps, can you tell us the bowler (seamer or spinner) who has the highest percentage of their balls bowled that would go on to hit the stumps?CricViz: In the ball-tracking era (since 2006) former Pakistan all-rounder Mohammad Hafeez has the highest percentage of balls projected to hit the stumps at 41%. When considering only pace bowlers, Paul Collingwood leads the way with just under 19% of his deliveries hitting the stumps.Tests in Bangladesh have the highest percentage of deliveries hitting the stumps at 27%, no surprise considering the amount of spin bowled. The fast and bouncy pitches of Australia have historically seen just 12% of deliveries hit the stumps, however, the lowest for any nation.Ben, Llangrannog: Which batter has had the greatest success with decision review system (DRS) reviews?CricViz: Of the 35 batters to have taken 15 or more reviews in all Tests since the start of 2016, Bangladesh's Liton Das has the highest success rate with 68.8% (11 out of 16) of his DRS reviews overturned by the umpire, followed by India's Cheteshwar Pujara with 60% (9 out of 15) and West Indies' Kraigg Brathwaite with 55.6% (10 out of 18).If you look at this from a bowler's perspective, of the 58 bowlers to have taken 15 or more reviews in all Tests since the start of 2016, West Indies' Kemar Roach has the highest success rate with 35% (14 out of 40) of his DRS reviews overturned by the umpire, followed by England's Chris Woakes with 29.4% (10 out of 34) and Stuart Broad with 29.1% (16 out of 55).Jack, Tanzania: If he continues at his current rate, when is Joe Root predicted to beat Tendulkar's run record in Test matches?CricViz: Joe Root is currently on 14,180 Test runs, 1,741 runs behind Sachin Tendulkar's tally of 15,921. In Tests since the start of 2024, Root has scored 2,794 runs in 32 Tests and 58 innings, scoring 47.6 runs per innings on average. If he continues scoring at the same rate, he will need another 37 innings to go past Tendulkar's run record. That could approximately be around 20 Tests.As of now, until the end of the next home summer in England, Root has another 14 Tests to go, with two more Tests left in this current series against Pakistan, three away Tests in South Africa in December and January 2027, two away Tests in Bangladesh in February 2027, a one-off 150th Anniversary Test match versus Australia at the MCG in March 2027, followed by one home Test versus Bangladesh at Lord's in May 2027, and the five Ashes Tests in June and August 2027.It could be 15 Tests until the end of the next summer if England convert their slim chance to qualify for the final of the World Test Championship (WTC).Current World Test Championship standingsFreddie Davidson, Northampton: Who has the highest average across all formats over the last 10 years, all-format player?CricViz: Since the start of 2016 in men's internationals, 43 players have scored at least 1,500 runs in men's Tests, 1,000 runs in ODIs and 500 runs in T20Is.Of these 43 players, Virat Kohli's average of 56.4 is the highest in these last 10 years. Kohli averages 48.3 in Tests, 67.6 in ODIs and 50.3 in T20Is.Joe Belham, Manchester: Is there any data to prove if left-handed or right-handed batters are better across the history of the sport? Commentators often suggest that left-handed batters are more attractive on the eye and I've always thought that must be nonsense!CricViz: Looking at this in terms of batting average, in all three international formats in both the men's and women's formats, left-handed batters fare better compared to right-handed batters (if we're looking at just the recognised batters playing in the top seven in the batting order).Ben Snowball, Surrey: At what specific pace (mph) has there been the most wickets in Test cricket for fast bowlers?CricViz: In Tests where ball-tracking data is available (since the start of 2006), if we break down all wickets in a 1mph range, deliveries from pace bowlers in the 84-85mph range have seen the most wickets with 1,594 in total. If you break the speeds down to a single decimal, 84.6 mph has been the most productive wicket-taking delivery with 193 wickets in total.Leo, London: In the wake of Bazball, I would love to see breakdowns of risk/reward for various players and various shots. In general, do you have statistics on outcomes for forward defensives, cuts, drives, hooks, pulls, etc?CricViz: Looking at the last three years of shot type data against pace in Test cricket, the dismissal rate for some 'attacking' shots is relatively similar to that of defensive strokes, with defensive shots seeing a dismissal every 41 deliveries, similar to that of cut shots (40.4 balls per dismissal) and flicks (38.1 balls per dismissal). While batters may be striking at 123 when driving, their dismissal rate sits at 31.9, 10 balls lower than that of defensive strokes. Hook (15 balls per dismissal) and pull (22.7 balls per dismissal) shots hover around the 150 mark in terms of strike-rate but with a much more frequent dismissal rate compared to defending.Batters are dismissed every 295.5 balls when leaving; a good leave is certainly the best shot in the book when it comes to keeping your wicket intact.Chris Crighton, Stanmore: What ball of the over takes the most wickets? My money is on the sixth!CricViz: Well, unfortunately it's not the sixth ball, Chris. In Test cricket, the second ball of the over has seen the most wickets fall on 11,866 occasions, followed by the fifth ball with 11,787 wickets. This takes into account Tests with such ball-by-ball data where we've had four balls, five balls and eight balls in an over and now finally settling to the standard six.Chris, Derbyshire: What is the most common score in Test match cricket (team and individual)?CricViz: Most common team score in Tests: 296 (44 instances), followed by 191 (43 instances) and then 223 (42 instances).Most common individual score in Tests: As expected, 0 with 11,877 instances followed by 1 (4,684 instances) and then 4 (3,897 instances). Note that the score of 0 here includes all instances of a batter coming to bat including dismissals and not outs.Ben, Natland: How many times did Mahendra Singh Dhoni hit a six to win a game? And is he the person to do this the most times?CricViz: MS Dhoni has hit a six to win an ODI or T20I on 12 occasions, the most by any batter in limited-overs in international cricket.Most instances to win a game with a six in run-chases in ODIs and T20Is:MS Dhoni - 12 (ODIs - 9, T20Is - 3)Virat Kohli - 9 (ODIs - 5, T20Is - 4)Eoin Morgan - 8 (ODIs - 3, T20Is - 5)Jos Buttler - 8 (ODIs - 5, T20Is - 3)Shoaib Malik - 7 (ODIs - 4, T20Is - 3)KL Rahul - 7 (ODIs - 6, T20Is - 1)

title: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit
description: Image source, Warwickshire County CouncilImage caption, Drivers have been asked to use alternative routesByShannen HeadleyWest MidlandsUpdated 39 minu
body: Image source, Warwickshire County CouncilImage caption, Drivers have been asked to use alternative routesByShannen HeadleyWest MidlandsUpdated 39 minutes agoA man has died and two women have been injured in a crash that followed a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics. The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said. Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.It has since reopened. Confirmed deceasedA spokesperson for West Midlands Ambulance Service said paramedics found four patients in total at the scene. They included a man who was in a critical condition to whom crews gave advanced life support."Despite their best efforts, it became clear that nothing more could be done to save him and he was confirmed deceased by ambulance staff at the scene," the spokesperson said.A woman who was driving the second car suffered life-threatening injuries, the ambulance service confirmed, and was taken to hospital in a critical condition. She was said by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to be in her 70s.A female passenger in the vehicle was also seriously hurt and taken to hospital, although her condition was not thought by the ambulance service to be life-threatening.Injuries to another patient from the car were not believed to be serious.InvestigationSupt Steve Flavell said: "Our thoughts are with the families of everyone involved in this collision and we're providing specialist support to them at this extremely difficult time."We made a mandatory referral to the IOPC because a death had occurred following police contact. "They have declared an independent investigation and we will co-operate fully with their investigation."The IOPC said the investigation was at an early stage and confirmed its officials attended the police's post-incident operation to gather information. "We understand the driver of a black Audi A3 failed to stop for police and was then pursued for around six minutes before the vehicle was involved in a collision with a car being driven by a member of the public," a spokesperson said.Works were carried out on Warwick Road two years ago, aimed at reducing the number of crashes in the area.Warwickshire County Council added a one-way system, lowered the speed limit and implemented a protected turning lane at the Ingon Lane junction.Street lighting was also boosted to improve visibility for crossing pedestrians at Fisherman's Car Park.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Coventry & Warwickshire

schema.headline: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit
